Poland Lifts Restrictions as Epidemic Subsides, Businesses Resume Activity

Poland has lifted its nationwide restrictions following the containment of the respiratory virus epidemic that swept the country over the past six weeks, officials announced on Monday. The measures, which included the temporary closure of non-essential businesses, strict curbs on travel between regions, and limitations on public gatherings, had a significant impact on economic activity across sectors ranging from construction to retail.

The government credited a combination of mass vaccination efforts, targeted testing, and localized containment zones with bringing the outbreak under control. “We are pleased to see the number of new cases fall below 100 per day for the first time since early March,” said Deputy Health Minister Monika Piotrowska at a press conference in Warsaw. “This allows us to safely proceed with the reopening of businesses and public spaces.”

Among the companies affected during the epidemic was Vinci SA, a major employer in the infrastructure and construction sector. With several ongoing projects across Poland, Vinci SA was forced to halt or scale back operations in compliance with the restrictions. Speaking on Tuesday, Tomasz Lewandowski, spokesperson for Vinci SA in Poland, remarked, “We welcome the government’s decision. Our teams are returning to sites this week, and we are committed to making up for lost time while prioritizing worker safety.”

Regional economic analysts estimate that the epidemic cost the national economy nearly 1.4 billion złoty per week in lost output, with construction, logistics, and hospitality among the hardest-hit. The Polish Chamber of Commerce praised the swift implementation of support measures such as wage subsidies and emergency grants, but warned of ongoing challenges. “Many small and medium enterprises still face cashflow issues,” said Chamber president Katarzyna Góralczyk. “It will take months for some sectors to fully recover.”

Local governments have begun reopening public transport and administrative offices, while schools and universities are scheduled to resume in-person classes next week. The Ministry of Health urged continued vigilance, recommending mask use in crowded indoor spaces and ongoing surveillance for possible new clusters of infection.

Despite the economic disruption, public health officials stress the success of the coordinated response. “This was a difficult period for everyone, but the resilience shown by our communities and businesses has been remarkable,” said Wojciech Baran, head of the National Public Health Institute.

As activity resumes, the government has pledged to review lessons from the epidemic and invest in strengthening Poland’s emergency preparedness for the future.
